common_name: California Blackeye Cowpea (Classic Commercial Black-Eyed Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; in zone 9, plant from late spring through midsummer for successive harvests, since California Blackeye thrives in peak summer heat.

directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after the soil has warmed, and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which promotes foliage at the expense of pod set. California Blackeye is an upright, semi-bush cowpea developed by University of California breeding programs and grown extensively as the standard commercial black-eyed pea, valued for its concentrated pod set that ripens fairly uniformly for efficient once-over harvest, along with good disease resistance and dependable yields. The classic cream-colored pea with its signature black eye has excellent flavor whether cooked fresh, dried for storage, or prepared in the traditional Southern black-eyed pea dishes served for New Year's luck. Like all cowpeas it fixes nitrogen in the soil and thrives in hot summer weather that stalls cooler-season legumes, making it a reliable, low-input crop for Gulf South vegetable gardens.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — cowpea variety records

common_name: Zipper Cream Cowpea (Easy-Shelling Cream Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; in zone 9, plant from late spring through midsummer, since Zipper Cream performs best in hot weather.

directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and harvest pods when they turn from green to a pale cream-tan color and feel plump. Zipper Cream is a beloved Southern heirloom cowpea named for its distinctive, easy-shelling pods — the seam splits open with a simple pinch or tug, quickly releasing rows of smooth, cream-white peas without the tedious shelling required by many other cowpea types. The mild, sweet, creamy flavor and tender texture of the peas make Zipper Cream one of the most popular fresh-shelling Southern peas for the table, while its productive, heat-loving vines perform reliably through the hottest stretch of summer when many other vegetables falter. As with all cowpeas, the roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, leaving the soil enriched for a following crop. Pick pods regularly at the cream stage for the best fresh-eating quality, or allow pods to dry fully on the vine for shelf-stable dried peas.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Zipper Cream cowpea variety notes

common_name: Whippoorwill Cowpea (Historic Speckled Southern Heirloom Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; Whippoorwill is a rangier, semi-vining heirloom that benefits from a bit more spacing than compact modern cowpea cultivars.

directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean soil in full sun, and avoid rich, heavily fertilized ground, which pushes vine growth at the expense of pod production in this vigorous heirloom. Whippoorwill is one of the oldest documented Southern cowpea varieties, grown since before the Civil War and named for its speckled brown-and-tan seed coat, which resembles the mottled plumage of the whippoorwill bird. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant, it was historically valued as a dual-purpose crop, grown both for its rich, earthy-flavored dried and fresh peas and as a soil-building, nitrogen-fixing cover crop plowed under to enrich depleted fields, a role it still serves well in a home garden rotation. Its tough constitution and long history make it a genuine piece of Southern agricultural heritage as well as a reliable, low-input summer crop. Harvest pods green for fresh shelling or let them dry fully on the vine for long-term storage.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Whippoorwill cowpea heritage notes
USDA National Genetic Resources Program — cowpea germplasm records

common_name: Texas Cream 40 Cowpea (Compact Early Cream Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; the compact, bush habit and short 55–65 day maturity make Texas Cream 40 well suited to successive plantings for an extended harvest through summer.

directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and harvest pods when they lighten from green to a pale cream color. Texas Cream 40 is a compact, bush-type cowpea bred for a short, roughly 55–65 day maturity and a concentrated pod set well suited to gardeners who want an early, efficient harvest without the sprawling vines of older heirloom cowpea types. The smooth, cream-colored peas have a mild, sweet flavor and tender texture prized for fresh shelling, and the plant's compact size makes it a good fit for smaller garden beds or closer spacing than rangier Southern pea varieties. Its short season also allows two or more successive plantings through the Gulf South summer for an extended harvest window. As with other cowpeas, the roots fix nitrogen, leaving the soil enriched for the next crop.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — cowpea variety trials
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database

common_name: Mississippi Silver Cowpea (Silver-Hulled Crowder Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; Mississippi Silver shows good resistance to common Southern pea diseases, making it a reliable choice for humid Gulf South gardens.

directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and harvest pods once they turn from green to a silvery, pale green-white color at the crowder stage. Mississippi Silver is a productive crowder-type cowpea whose closely packed, squarish peas fill the pod so tightly they are pressed ('crowded') against one another, developing a rich, hearty flavor prized in traditional Southern cooking. Its pale, silvery pod color at harvest makes ripeness easy to spot, and the variety is noted for good tolerance to common cowpea diseases and heat stress, producing reliably through the hottest part of the Gulf South summer when many other vegetables decline. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil for whatever crop follows. Harvest continuously at the silver-green stage for fresh shelling, or allow pods to dry fully for long-term storage.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension — cowpea variety notes
